en_alt: He was sitting at the back.
He sat behind.
note: Imperfective сидел also reads as a progressive; both renderings are valid.

en_alt: The rain was falling very heavily.
It was raining very heavily.
note: шёл is imperfective, so the progressive is at least as accurate as the simple past.

en_alt: The wind is blowing more strongly than in the morning.
note: Russian present tense is equally the English progressive here.

en_alt: Most likely he is already at home.
note: «до́ма» is equally 'at home'; the comma is optional in English.

en_alt: Hurry up and come here!
Come here, quick!
note: 'Come here quicker' is not idiomatic English; скорее in an imperative means 'quickly / hurry'.

en: This is more of a joke than the truth.
en_alt: This is more a joke than the truth.
note: 'rather a joke than the truth' is not an English construction; the comparative frame is 'more … than'.

en_alt: Come soon, we are waiting.
note: 'Come sooner' implies an earlier alternative that isn't there; скорее with an imperative urges speed.

en_alt: Without books the journey is more boring.
note: A second natural rendering of the impersonal comparative.

en_alt: In the lesson it is boring without games.
note: The literal impersonal structure is worth accepting alongside the recast subject.

en: The shop is to the left of the station.
en_alt: The shop is located to the left of the station.
note: With «сле́ва от X» English says 'to the left of X'; 'on the left of the station' reads as part of the station.

en_alt: To my left sat a friend.
A friend sat on my left.
note: Russian fronts the place phrase; both English orders are valid.

en_alt: On the left there is a big house.
note: «стои́т» for a building is normally rendered 'there is' in English.

en_alt: You are speaking too quickly.
note: Russian present covers both English presents.

ru: Ты случа́йно не зна́ешь его́ а́дрес?
en_alt: You don't happen to know his address, do you?
note: The Russian «случа́йно не» tag is idiomatic; both English hedges are correct.

en_alt: I cannot hear you at all.
You can't be heard at all.
note: The impersonal is normally said in the first person in English.

en_alt: I find his jokes funny.
note: A closer rendering of the dative-experiencer construction.

en: The clown fell in a funny way.
en_alt: The clown had a funny fall.
note: 'fell funnily' is not something an English speaker writes; the manner adverb has to be periphrastic here.

en_alt: The building looks old from the outside.
note: Both English orders are equally natural.

en_alt: Let's start over.
Let us start from the beginning.
note: «снача́ла» here is 'from the start', and 'start over' is the everyday equivalent.

en_alt: It began to rain again.
It started raining again.
note: Inchoative пошёл has several equally natural English renderings.

en_alt: As a matter of fact, he is right.
Actually speaking, he is right.
note: «со́бственно говоря́» covers both 'strictly speaking' and 'as a matter of fact'.

en_alt: What do you actually want?
note: The plainer question is an equally valid rendering of the parenthetical.
«совсе́м молода́я» intensifies, but British 'quite young' hedges downward and weakens it.

en_alt: According to the plan, we will set off in the morning.
note: «вы́едем» is specifically setting off by vehicle; both renderings work.

en: First we ate, then we went for a walk.
en_alt: First we ate, then we strolled.
note: «гуля́ли» is going for a walk / strolling, not simply 'walked' (which suggests locomotion to somewhere).

en_alt: He deliberately said it loudly.
He said it loudly deliberately.
note: «специа́льно» here is 'deliberately / on purpose'; both are natural.

en_alt: I came to you specially.
note: The literal 'came to you' matches «к тебе́» without the added 'see'.

en_alt: This gift is specially for you.
note: 'present' and 'gift' are both пода́рок.

en_alt: The child was sleeping peacefully.
The child slept calmly.
note: Imperfective спал equally supports the progressive.

en_alt: You can work calmly here.
note: Impersonal мо́жно is normally 'you can' in everyday English.

en_alt: On the right a river is roaring.
A river is making noise on the right.
note: «шуми́т» is making noise/roaring; 'rushing' adds motion the Russian does not state, so alternatives help.

en_alt: You will see a pharmacy on the right.
note: Both English orders are equally natural.

en_alt: I recognised him immediately.
I immediately recognised him.
note: Equivalent renderings of сра́зу.

en_alt: Call me immediately after the lesson.
note: 'right after' and 'immediately after' are both сра́зу по́сле.

en_alt: I need a doctor urgently.
note: Adverb placement is free in English here.

en_alt: Urgently call home.
Call home immediately.
note: The Russian fronts сро́чно; the English can too.

ru: Я не ожида́ла столь тёплого приёма.
Э́то столь же ва́жно, как и пре́жде.
en_alt: This is just as important as it was before.
note: Both English forms of the equative are natural.

en_alt: I had not seen so many people.
note: Russian past with не supports either English perfect or pluperfect reading.

en_alt: Do not eat so many sweets.
note: Uncontracted form for the word-bank drill.

en_alt: It is strange that he is still not here.
note: «ещё нет» reads as either 'not yet' or 'still not'.

en_alt: The car is making a strange noise.
note: Russian present equally supports the progressive.

en_alt: I am frightened on my own in the dark.
note: «одному́» is 'alone / on my own'; the masculine dative is not visible in English.

en_alt: You have to speak more strictly with children.
note: Impersonal на́до is more usually 'you have to' than 'one has to' in everyday English.

en_alt: Mum talked to him sternly.
note: 'spoke strictly with him' is not idiomatic; English collocates 'sternly' with manner of speaking, as the sibling sentence already does.

en_alt: It is strictly forbidden to smoke here.
note: The literal impersonal matches the Russian word order.

en_alt: It is shameful to talk to your mother like that.
note: 'speak to' and 'talk to' are both «говори́ть с».

en_alt: The boy grew ashamed.
note: 'became ashamed' is stilted; English expresses the inchoative dative state as 'felt ashamed'.

en_alt: Are you not ashamed?
note: Uncontracted form for the word-bank drill.

ru: У нас и так ма́ло вре́мени.
en_alt: We have little time as it is anyway.
We already have little time as it is.
note: «и так» is the 'as it is / anyway' particle; the current rendering is right, alternatives help the drill.

en_alt: Do it just as I do.
Do it the same way I do.
note: «как я» is elliptical and takes several English forms.

en_alt: Something here is wrong.
Something is not right here.
note: «не так» is literally 'not right'; both are idiomatic.

ru: Он так уста́л, что усну́л сра́зу.

en_alt: Not so quickly!
note: «бы́стро» is glossed 'quickly' corpus-wide.

ru: Мы купи́ли хлеб и та́кже молоко́.
Он зна́ет неме́цкий, а та́кже францу́зский.
en_alt: He knows German, as well as French.
note: «а та́кже» is regularly 'as well as'.

ru: Я та́кже хочу́ пойти́ с ва́ми.
Мы встре́тимся там же, где и вчера́.
en_alt: We will meet in the same place as yesterday.
note: 'at the same place' and 'in the same place' are both natural.

en_alt: It got dark outside.
note: 'got dark' is the everyday equivalent of ста́ло темно́.

ru: В лесу́ темне́е, чем в по́ле.

en_alt: What are we going to do now?
What will we do now?
note: Compound future бу́дем де́лать maps to several English futures.

en_alt: Dress warmly, it is freezing outside.
note: Uncontracted form for the word-bank drill.

ru: В ку́ртке тепле́е, чем в сви́тере.

en_alt: They greeted us warmly.
note: The Russian is an active third-person plural; the active English is at least as literal.

ru: В це́ркви на́до вести́ себя́ ти́хо.
en_alt: In church one must behave quietly.
note: Impersonal на́до takes either 'you' or 'one'.
Comparative ти́ше is correctly 'more quietly', which keeps it distinct from the вы-form sibling.

en_alt: He is the only one who can do this.
note: Current English is correct; the cleft is an equally common rendering.

en_alt: I understood everything immediately.
I immediately understood everything.
note: The headword gloss is 'immediately'; that rendering should be accepted too.

en_alt: The doctor arrived immediately.
note: «прие́хал» is specifically arriving by transport, so 'arrived' is the closer verb.

en_alt: He answered the letter immediately.
note: Adverb placement is free in English.

en_alt: He will definitely arrive tomorrow.
note: «прие́дет» is arriving by transport; 'arrive' is closer than 'come'.

en_alt: The clock shows the time exactly.
The clock keeps time accurately.
note: The headword gloss 'exactly' should be accepted alongside 'precisely'.

en: I know the answer for sure.
en_alt: I know the answer for certain.
note: «то́чно зна́ю» is 'know for sure/for certain'; 'know the answer exactly' reads as knowing its precise wording.

en_alt: It is hard for the patient to breathe.
note: The literal impersonal-dative structure matches the Russian and is natural English.

en_alt: It is difficult for him to speak Russian.
note: 'hard' and 'difficult' both render тру́дно.

en_alt: It is difficult to live without money.
note: 'hard' and 'difficult' both render тру́дно.

en_alt: It is hard for me to understand this rule.
note: 'hard' and 'difficult' both render тру́дно.

ru: Мы е́дем туда́ же, куда́ и вчера́.
en_alt: We are driving to the same place as yesterday.
note: «е́дем» is specifically by transport, which the current English leaves implicit.

en: We are going there on foot.
en_alt: We are walking there.
note: 'walking there on foot' is redundant in English; идём carries the going, пешко́м the manner.

en_alt: This suitcase is heavy for me to carry.
note: «тяжело́» here carries its literal weight sense, which the headword gloss 'heavily' covers.

en_alt: It is surprising how quickly time flies.
note: The gloss-matching 'surprising / quickly' rendering is equally natural and should be accepted.

en_alt: Today it is surprisingly warm.
note: The Russian fronts сего́дня; both English orders are natural.
